summary:
We built Trend Atlas, an interactive web app for investigating how Earth’s temperature and rainfall have changed over time. For the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge, we wanted people to start with a place they were curious about, pick a time period, and see what NASA’s observations could tell them. Users can select regions on a 3D globe or flat map, compare their trends, and see how certain the estimates are.

In our polar comparison, the Arctic latitude band warmed about 0.59 °C per decade faster than the Antarctic band from 2001 to 2024. The Arctic increase was clear, while the Antarctic trend on its own was inconclusive for that period. Trend Atlas makes that distinction visible and lets students, educators, and other users inspect the underlying observations and download the evidence.
details:
Trend Atlas starts with a question you can ask right on the map. Pick a region, choose a dataset and time period, and the dashboard shows the selected year’s value alongside the longer-term trend. Add a second region and the app compares them over the same years. The globe can expand for closer inspection or switch to a flat map. The dashboard uses warmer colors for supported increases, cooler colors for supported decreases, and a neutral background when the evidence is inconclusive. The result is also written out, so you can read it without relying on color.

Under the hood, we used React, TypeScript, and Vite for the interface, MapLibre GL for the map and globe, and Apache ECharts for charts. A Python and FastAPI backend processes NASA’s temperature tables and gridded data, along with rainfall data obtained through NASA Giovanni for northern and southeastern Australia. We used statsmodels to fit trends and calculate 95% confidence intervals that account for possible correlation between nearby years. When comparing two regions, the app calculates their difference for each year and fits a trend to that series.

One decision we kept coming back to was how to show uncertainty clearly. A line can slope upward even when the evidence is too weak to support an increase. The app explains that distinction and flags windows with too few consecutive years for inference. Students can start with the map and a plain-language result. Anyone who wants to reproduce the analysis can inspect the observations, units, baseline, and method, then export the evidence as a CSV.
